reference.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies / WHO envenoming guidance
clinicalPearls: Stonefish (Synanceia) have dorsal spines that inject venom when trodden on, causing immediate and often excruciating pain out of proportion to the wound
Local effects include intense pain, rapid swelling, discolouration and sometimes tissue necrosis, with retained spine fragments a common complication
Hot-water immersion of the affected part at a tolerable temperature is a key first-aid measure, as the venom is heat-labile and this can relieve pain
Systemic features may include nausea, sweating, weakness and, uncommonly, cardiovascular and respiratory effects with severe envenomation
Stonefish antivenom is available and used for severe pain or systemic envenomation; wound exploration for retained spine and foreign material is important
Secondary wound infection is common, so wound care, tetanus prophylaxis and monitoring for infection including marine organisms are essential
Distinguish envenomation pain and swelling from evolving secondary soft-tissue infection during follow-up
reference.pathophysiology: Stonefish venom, delivered through grooved dorsal spines, contains a pore-forming protein (verrucotoxin/stonustoxin family) that disrupts cell membranes and causes intense local pain, oedema and potential tissue necrosis. Systemic absorption can produce cardiovascular effects including hypotension and arrhythmia, and the venom has actions on skeletal and cardiac muscle. Many venom components are heat-labile, which underlies the analgesic benefit of hot-water immersion. Puncture wounds frequently retain spine fragments and are prone to secondary infection by marine and skin flora.
additionalDifferentials: Other venomous fish spine injury (lionfish, scorpionfish, weeverfish, stingray)
Simple puncture wound with secondary infection
Marine bacterial infection (e.g. Vibrio, Mycobacterium marinum)
additionalInvestigations: Wound imaging (ultrasound or radiography) to detect retained spine fragments
Assessment of neurovascular status of the affected limb
Electrocardiography and monitoring in systemic envenomation
Inflammatory markers and wound cultures if infection is suspected
Renal function and creatine kinase in severe systemic cases
redFlags: Systemic features such as hypotension, arrhythmia or respiratory compromise
Signs of compartment syndrome or extensive necrosis
Spreading soft-tissue infection or systemic sepsis
Retained deep foreign material near neurovascular structures
Uncontrolled severe pain despite first aid
reference.prognosis: Most stings cause severe transient pain that improves with hot-water immersion and analgesia, with full recovery. Complications arise chiefly from retained spines, secondary infection and, rarely, systemic envenomation; delayed or inadequate wound care prolongs morbidity.
pitfalls: Using very hot water that scalds the anaesthetised, painful limb
Missing retained spine fragments leading to persistent pain and infection
Neglecting tetanus prophylaxis and marine wound care
Attributing later worsening solely to venom rather than recognising secondary infection
management: Immediate hot-water immersion at a tolerable temperature to inactivate the heat-labile venom and relieve pain
Stonefish antivenom for severe pain unresponsive to immersion or for systemic envenomation
Local anaesthetic infiltration or regional block with systemic analgesia for pain control
Wound exploration and removal of retained spine fragments and foreign material
Tetanus prophylaxis and antibiotics covering marine organisms where infection risk is high or established
Cardiac monitoring and supportive care for cardiovascular and respiratory effects in systemic envenomation
Surgical review for deep wounds and ongoing monitoring for secondary infection and necrosis
